newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - MOUNTAINEERING - British climber aims for six-peak Himalayan record.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - MOUNTAINEERING - British climber aims for six-peak Himalayan record.

text.p: British climber Alan Hinkes sets out on Wednesday to win a place among the giants of mountaineering by tackling a challenge no one has tried before -- to scale six of the world's 8,000 metre peaks in less than a year.
If he succeeds he will be the first person in Britain, and only the sixth in the world, to have climbed all 14 of the world's deadly 8,000 metre (26,246 feet) peaks.
"No one has even attempted six in a year and it is a hell of a challenge. It's taken me 10 years to do the last eight," he told Reuters in an interview shortly before his departure.

Hinkes's bid for the record books will start on the ice-blasted slopes of Nepal's 8,516 metre (27,940 feet) Lhotse. From there he will travel to base camp for the 8,463 metre (27,765 feet) Makalu in Nepal, flying by helicopter to keep his body accustomed to the high altitudes.
He will climb alone, without bottled oxygen.
"The odds are stacked against him," said Roger Payne of the British Mountaineering Council.
The 14 peaks, of which Hinkes has already climbed eight, have exacted a vicious toll on the world's climbers.

The most feared is the second highest -- Pakistan's K2 at 8,611 metres (28,251 feet). Known as Savage Mountain, roughly one climber in every three who has tried to reach its summit has died in the attempt.
Hinkes, from the northern English county of Yorkshire, reached the top of K2 in 1995 after three assaults.
"K2 is the prize in mountaineering. It's much more difficult than Everest as it's got steeper slopes, more avalanche danger, more rockfall danger, and worse weather."
Last year he climbed Everest. The world's highest mountain, at 8,848 metres (29,028 feet), is relatively safe -- at around one death in every seven or eight attempts to climb it.
THE MOUNTAIN HE FEARS THE MOST

In Hinkes's current challenge the 8,586 metre (28,169 feet) Kanchenjunga in Nepal is technically the most difficult, with a 100 metre (330 feet) near-vertical section at the top. But he fears Makalu the most.
"Makalu is my bogey mountain and psychologically could be the most difficult."

On a previous attempt on Makalu Hinkes was 100 metres from the summit when his companion, British climber Rick Allen, fell 400 metres (440 feet). He survived because the snow cushioned his fall and Hinkes was able to rescue him from 7,800 metres (25,590 feet). On his next attempt Hinkes slipped on his way to base camp and the branch of a tree speared his thigh through a wound the size of his hand. He was alone on the path.
"I was getting a bit fed up by this stage," he said. "I had a couple of paracetamol and a twig to bite on so I crawled back to the nearest telephone -- 12 hours away."
He said he had succeeded to date because he had been ready to back off. "But also I am determined -- I am a Yorkshireman."
"The biggest danger has been people's misjudgement of their own abilities. They push too far, too hard, on climbs where they think the summit is the end, rather than the half-way point."

Despite the large number of widely-publicised climbing deaths last year -- 11 died on Everest in May alone -- Hinkes does not feel the need to defend mountaineering against its critics. Nor does he advocate tighter restrictions on such climbs.
"Why the hell should I justify it? It's no different to being a soccer player or a racing driver -- and what actual use are they? I am no use either.
"But we entertain people, -- the public does not want to do these things but they do like heroes that do them for them.
"I don't think there should be restrictions, either. What it is all about is freedom -- and that means a lack of restriction."

He said the dangers were the ferocious weather and snow conditions such as wind slab -- snow which feels deceptively hard but is soft underneath. "If you walk across it your footprints make perforations in it like toilet paper, and it can tear off."
"In my case I think I know when enough is enough. No mountain is worth a life."
